memory_update.text: Add ORCL as a direct AI compute-demand platform candidate; key evidence is FY2026 RPO scale and AI/cloud infrastructure capacity risk disclosures.
Add CRWV as a high-purity AI cloud/neocloud candidate; evidence strength is high, but concentration, leverage and deployment execution must be tracked.

Add IREN as a vertically integrated AI cloud and power-backed data-center candidate; high relevance but a portion of projected economics remains uncontracted and should be treated as execution-sensitive.
Add DELL as a scaled AI server infrastructure supplier with unusually large disclosed AI server orders, shipments and backlog.
Add DLR as a data-center REIT/asset-owner candidate tied to scarce hyperscale AI-oriented capacity, leasing backlog and powered campus expansion.

Later Layer 1B passes should separately test other possible direct or near-direct names: EQIX, SMCI, HPE, APLD, WULF, NBIS, CLS, and major utilities/power developers tied to data-center interconnection queues.

CRWV and NBIS are direct public AI-cloud capacity plays for the hyperscaler/AI compute-demand node; monitor customer concentration, contracted power, funding and utilization rather than treating revenue growth alone as proof of bottleneck capture.
FIX and MOD are second-order infrastructure suppliers tied to the physical conversion of AI capex into deployable clusters; backlog, data-center mix and margin resilience are the key evidence gates.

BE is a higher-risk chokepoint candidate because onsite power is highly relevant to grid-constrained AI data centers, but commercial adoption, permitting, financing and fuel economics need stronger validation.

Additional names for later passes: Powell Industries, nVent, Bel Fuse, Bloom-adjacent electrical integrators, transformer/switchgear vendors, data-center REITs, colocation providers, and private neoclouds such as Lambda where public-market mappings are indirect.
CRWV should be tracked as a direct public AI-cloud demand aggregator with very large RPO but high sensitivity to financing, customer concentration, GPU supply and deployment timing.
NBIS is a less obvious neocloud candidate with explicit Microsoft GPU-capacity agreement evidence and additional relevance to sovereign/regional AI infrastructure.
APLD maps to hyperscaler AI data-center outsourcing and the power/construction/financing bottleneck rather than to software or chips.
CLS offers underappreciated exposure to the physical server, rack, optical and networking hardware required to convert AI capex into deployed clusters.
BE should be monitored as an adjacent time-to-power chokepoint beneficiary after explicit Oracle and Nebius AI infrastructure power agreements.

Future Layer 1B passes should separately test electrical contractors and MEP firms such as FIX, IESC and EME; nuclear/IPPs such as TLN; and AI networking component suppliers such as CRDO, COHR and LITE.

node: Hyperscaler, AI cloud and sovereign AI compute demand
summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Expanded the US-listed universe for the AI compute-demand node beyond the seed hyperscalers. The strongest additions are companies that either own AI cloud capacity, sell deployable AI server systems, or own scarce powered data-center capacity. Priority candidates for later evidence work: Oracle as a hyperscale AI cloud platform with large AI/cloud backlog; CoreWeave and IREN as AI cloud/neocloud capacity owners; Dell as a scaled AI-optimized server supplier to neocloud, sovereign, enterprise and cloud customers; and Digital Realty as a large data-center asset owner with hyperscale AI-oriented leasing evidence. This is research support only, not a trading recommendation. Expanded the universe around scarce capacity and deployment bottlenecks for hyperscaler, AI-cloud and sovereign compute demand. The strongest incremental candidates are direct AI-cloud capacity providers and second-order physical-infrastructure suppliers tied to power, cooling, mechanical/electrical construction and onsite generation. This pass intentionally avoids buy/sell conclusions and treats each name as a research candidate requiring customer, backlog, margin and deployment-timing verification. Expanded the universe around the demand node toward neocloud capacity lessors, AI data-center developers, outsourced server/network hardware build partners, and on-site power providers. The common chokepoint is hyperscalers' ability to turn AI capex into live GPU clusters despite constraints in GPUs, power, data-center shells, MEP labor, networking hardware, and customer concentration. This is research support
